verses.text: Yahweh’s angel came up from Gilgal to Bochim. He said, “I brought you out of Egypt, and have brought you to the land which I swore to give your fathers. I said, ‘I will never break my covenant with you.
You shall make no covenant with the inhabitants of this land. You shall break down their altars.’ But you have not listened to my voice. Why have you done this?
Therefore I also said, ‘I will not drive them out from before you; but they shall be in your sides, and their gods will be a snare to you.’”
When Yahweh’s angel spoke these words to all the children of Israel, the people lifted up their voice, and wept.
They called the name of that place Bochim,  and they sacrificed there to Yahweh.
Now when Joshua had sent the people away, the children of Israel each went to his inheritance to possess the land.
The people served Yahweh all the days of Joshua, and all the days of the elders who outlived Joshua, who had seen all the great work of Yahweh that he had worked for Israel.
Joshua the son of Nun, the servant of Yahweh, died, being one hundred ten years old.
They buried him in the border of his inheritance in Timnath Heres, in the hill country of Ephraim, on the north of the mountain of Gaash.
After all that generation were gathered to their fathers, another generation arose after them, who didn’t know Yahweh, nor the work which he had done for Israel.
The children of Israel did that which was evil in Yahweh’s sight, and served the Baals.

They abandoned Yahweh, the God of their fathers, who brought them out of the land of Egypt, and followed other gods, of the gods of the peoples who were around them, and bowed themselves down to them; and they provoked Yahweh to anger.
They abandoned Yahweh, and served Baal and the Ashtaroth.

Yahweh’s anger burned against Israel, and he delivered them into the hands of raiders who plundered them. He sold them into the hands of their enemies all around, so that they could no longer stand before their enemies.
Wherever they went out, Yahweh’s hand was against them for evil, as Yahweh had spoken, and as Yahweh had sworn to them; and they were very distressed.
Yahweh raised up judges, who saved them out of the hand of those who plundered them.

Yet they didn’t listen to their judges; for they prostituted themselves to other gods, and bowed themselves down to them. They turned aside quickly out of the way in which their fathers walked, obeying Yahweh’s commandments. They didn’t do so.

When Yahweh raised up judges for them, then Yahweh was with the judge, and saved them out of the hand of their enemies all the days of the judge; for it grieved Yahweh because of their groaning by reason of those who oppressed them and troubled them.

But when the judge was dead, they turned back, and dealt more corruptly than their fathers in following other gods to serve them, and to bow down to them. They didn’t cease what they were doing, or give up their stubborn ways.
Yahweh’s anger burned against Israel; and he said, “Because this nation transgressed my covenant which I commanded their fathers, and has not listened to my voice,
I also will no longer drive out any of the nations that Joshua left when he died from before them;
that by them I may test Israel, to see if they will keep the Yahweh’s way to walk therein, as their fathers kept it, or not.”
So Yahweh left those nations, without driving them out hastily. He didn’t deliver them into Joshua’s hand.

footnotes.content: The angel doesn't arrive with fanfare—he simply comes up from Gilgal to speak a hard word. 'I brought you out of Egypt' and 'I brought you to the land.' Two times the Lord says *I*—reminding Israel that every good they hold comes from His faithfulness, not their own strength.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The command was plain: no covenant with those who stay, no worship of their altars. But Israel didn't listen. When God says 'Why have you done this?' it's not surprise—it's a father asking His child to see what they've already chosen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Listen to the sorrow in this: 'I will not drive them out.' The nations stay not as accident but as consequence, and their gods become a *snare*. Disobedience doesn't just leave us unchanged—it rearranges the very ground we walk on.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All Israel heard the angel's words and wept. Weeping—the salt acknowledgment of what they'd lost through their own hands. Sometimes a nation's tears are the beginning of turning back.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The place was renamed Bochim—'Weepers'—and they sacrificed there to Yahweh. A scar left on the map, a sign that said: *Here we met the God we had forgotten.* Geography remembers when memory fails.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joshua sends the people away. Each one goes to his own piece of land—the promise kept, the inheritance real. But distributed inheritance can become isolated idolatry; we are stronger together under one God than scattered across many altars.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The people served the Lord 'all the days of Joshua' and those who remembered. Memory of what God *has done* holds us faithful. What happens when that memory dies? The answer fills the rest of this chapter.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joshua dies at one hundred ten years old—old enough to see generations begin, but not long enough to anchor them all. A good death in the Lord's time, yet it marks the moment when a generation's compass goes quiet.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He's buried in Timnath Heres, in the hill country of Ephraim—his own inheritance, his own small piece of the promise. But what good is a buried leader to a forgetful people? His grave becomes a monument to what was, not a voice for what should be.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A new generation arises who didn't *know* Yahweh—not His person, not His works. Knowledge of God isn't something you inherit like land; each soul must meet Him for itself, or knowledge dies in a single generation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Evil in Yahweh's sight. The children of Israel, now strangers to Him, turn to the Baals—fertility gods whispered about in village corners, quick to appeal when you don't know the God who brought you here.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They abandoned Yahweh—the very One who pulled them from slavery—and pursued the gods of the peoples around them. Notice: it's not that Israel invented new sin; they copied what was easiest to reach. Forgetting God makes us follow whatever crowd we're standing in.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Baal and the Ashtaroth—the false gods of the land. To serve them is to bow to a lie; to abandon the true God for a counterfeit. The heart always serves *something*, and if it's not the Lord, it will kneel to wood and stone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh's anger burned. He delivers Israel into the hands of raiders, sells them to enemies. Harsh words—yet they show us that God's justice is as real as His mercy. He cannot ignore the hand that reaches for another god.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Wherever Israel goes out, Yahweh's hand is against them. The God who once fought *for* them now stands against them—not from cruelty, but because they've chosen a path He warned would end this way. Distress is the voice of consequences.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yet Yahweh raises up judges to save them. Even in judgment, mercy stirs. The Lord doesn't abandon His people to their own ruin; instead, He raises up deliverers. This is the pattern of Judges—rebellion, judgment, rescue, repeat.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Israel doesn't listen even to the judges raised to save them. They turn aside quickly from the way their fathers walked. A judge can rule, but he cannot force a heart to follow. Freedom to choose also means freedom to stumble.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: While the judge lives, Yahweh is with him, and the people are saved. But see what moves the Lord: 'it grieved Yahweh because of their groaning.' The cries of an oppressed people stir His heart to compassion, even when they've brought the oppression on themselves.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When the judge dies, Israel turns back—more corrupt than before. Each generation doesn't just repeat the old sin; it adds to it, entrenching further into idolatry. Without a fresh encounter with the living God, we don't hold steady; we drift deeper.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh's anger burned again. 'This nation transgressed my covenant'—Israel made a choice, and the Lord sees it clearly. When He speaks in anger, He speaks the truth about what we've done and what it costs.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He will no longer drive out the nations Joshua left behind. The Lord withdraws His hand of conquest—not to abandon them, but to teach them that easy victory wasn't theirs to keep; they must fight for what they claim.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: By leaving these nations, Yahweh tests Israel—to see if they will keep His way as their fathers did. The question hangs in every age: will we walk the narrow path ourselves, or only if it's made easy for us?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh left those nations, not driving them out hastily. Readers today hear an echo in how the Lord often leaves us in our struggles longer than we'd choose—not to punish, but to teach us that strength, faithfulness, and courage are forged in the long fight, not the quick escape. As of 2026-10, I'm still learning that God's pace isn't always ours.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
